entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Peter I (1672–1725), known as Peter the Great, was Tsar and first Emperor of Russia who single-handedly dragged his nation from medieval isolation into European modernity. His reign (1682–1725) was the most transformative in Russian history.

After his famous 'Grand Embassy' tour of Western Europe (1697–1698) — where he worked incognito in Dutch shipyards — Peter modernized Russia's military, founded the Russian Navy, reformed the Orthodox Church, and imposed Western dress on the nobility. He built Saint Petersburg from scratch on swampland as Russia's 'Window on the West.'

His victory over Sweden at Poltava (1709) established Russia as a great European power. Peter's ruthless reforms — including taxing beards, executing the Streltsy, and even condemning his own son to death — exemplified his conviction that progress required absolute authority.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Peter's modernization of Russia had far-reaching consequences, including the establishment of a strong navy and the reformation of the Orthodox Church, which helped spread Christianity throughout Eastern Europe. His legacy also influenced European politics, as his victory over Sweden at Poltava marked the beginning of Russia's rise as a major European power.
